newsitem.title: USA: Treasuries slump at signs of tight labor market.
newsitem.headline: Treasuries slump at signs of tight labor market.

text.p: Prices of Treasury securities fell Thursday for the third time in four sessions after a sharp drop in weekly jobless claims pointed to persistent strength in the nation's labour markets.

The drop in new jobless claims set the tone from the outset and prices were unable to recover despite reports that the Federal Reserve was buying short-maturity Treasuries for the second day in a row.

The benchmark 6.75 percent 30-year bond fell 8/32 to 98-23/32, raising its yield, which moves in the opposite direction from the price, to 6.85 percent from 6.83 percent on Wednesday. The 5.875 percent two-year note closed down 1/32 at 99-28/32 to yield 5.94 percent.

The Labour Department reported that first-time claims for state unemployment benefits fell by a hefty 22,000 in the week ended Oct. 19, to 320,000 from 342,000 the previous week. It was the lowest since claims touched 317,000 in the week ended Aug. 31.
The drop took Wall Street economists by surprise and reminded investors that the labour market remains tight, which could mean upward pressure on wages and prices.

"We know the labour market is pretty strong and the claims number reminded us of that," said Josh Feinman, vice president and global markets economist at Bankers Trust. "It was a holiday week so the data might be a little tougher to read but there's no question that the labour market is still strong."

In addition to the Columbus Day holiday, economists said the ripple effects of the recent strike by Canadian auto workers against General Motors Corp. in Canada also may have had an impact on the data.
Regardless of any distortions, many said they expected claims to bounce back from their low levels next week.
With prices lingering in negative territory in the aftermath of the claims report, traders said the Fed entered the market, buying two-year, three-year and five-year paper.
"It looked like the Fed came in under the table once again and took the market off its lows," said Theodore Ake, senior vice president and senior trader at Everen Securities Corp.
However, Ake said the Fed-induced price rise was fleeting, giving the market little more than a temporary push up from session lows.

Further weighing on the market Thursday was ongoing apprehension about upcoming economic data. The report on September durable goods orders, due on Friday, is expected to show a rebound from weak August numbers.
Meanwhile, widely divergent forecasts for the October employment report, due the following Friday, have also created some jitters in the market.
"I think there is a lot of nervousness and concern about next week's numbers," said Marilyn Schaja, money market economist at Donaldson, Lufkin and Jenrette Securities Corp.
In the corporate bond market, trading revolved around Tele-Communications Inc. as it has every day this week, dealers said.
TCI debt was hit early after the company said it has told suppliers to stop all shipments until further notice, traders said.

Prices bounced sharply higher after TCI said it expected to post third quarter revenues of $1.648 billion and operating cash flow of $591 million, traders said, but quickly faded below Wednesday's closing levels.

TCI's 7-7/8 percent debt due 2026 traded as wide as 285 basis points over the Treasury curve in early trade. The debt rebounded to a spread of 265 after the TCI announcement but was quoted at 280 near the close, five to 10 basis points wider on the day.
A flood of new issues clipped U.S. municipal bonds by 1/4 to 1/2 of a point, leaving traders fretting that yields might have to rise 10 to 15 basis points for the market to absorb next week's sales.

Issuers plan to sell at least $4 billion of municipal bonds next week, while at the short-end of the yield curve, the California Regents System expects to sell a total of $660 million of commercial paper in two deals.

While retail investors this week bought notes with maturities of up to seven years and institutional players snapped up long-term bonds, little interest was seen in the intermediate sector, traders said.

In another sign of weaker prices for intermediate issues, the calculation of the yield on the Reuters 10-year index of general obligation bonds rose three basis points to 5.06 percent from last Thursday.
